1:
The vague date is the first difficulty. Augustine holds that the phrase covers a far wider space than the fifteenth year named in the third Gospel, reaching from the birth to the preaching of John rather than to the childhood alone, which is what allows the return from Egypt and the twelve-year-old in the temple to stand together. Barnes reasons from the ages instead, that the days of the preceding chapter cannot be meant since John was only six months the elder, and puts the unrecorded interval at twenty-five years or more. Calvin fixes it by the reigns, John being about thirty and Tiberius fifteen years in power, and draws the consequence that the office was short: the morning star gave way that the Sun of Righteousness might shine alone.

Henry dwells on the silence that preceded it. Nothing is recorded of either child but the disputing with the doctors, and the heir while under age differs nothing from a servant; He turns it to two uses, that faith should look to Christ in his office rather than in his person, and that young men however well qualified should be slow to put themselves forward. He adds that after Malachi there had been no prophet for above three hundred years, so that the great prophet might be the more desired.

Why a herald was needed at all is Chrysostom's question. He gives three reasons: that Christ's dignity might appear, since he too has prophets; that the Jews might have no pretext, who complained of the one that he came neither eating nor drinking and of the other that he came eating and drinking; and that the witness should come from another mouth, since they afterwards objected that a man bearing witness of himself bears no true witness. He adds that John preached what they had never heard even from the prophets, and so gained their attention by the strangeness of it.

On the title itself Gregory and Bede work the same figure from opposite ends. Gregory argues from the relation of voice to word: the Son is called the Word of the Father, and as our own speech is known by the sounding of the voice, so John is the voice by whose ministry the Father's word is heard, crying in the desert because he shows forlorn Judaea her approaching consolation. Bede grants that the same cry has sounded from the beginning through everyone who spoke by inspiration, and finds the distinction elsewhere: John alone is called the voice because he declares as near what the others showed afar off.

Repentance draws the sharpest language. Robertson calls the English word the worst translation in the New Testament, since it means to be sorry again while the Greek means to change the mind and the conduct; the word that does mean sorrow is used of Judas, and he thinks the old Syriac turn ye nearer. Clarke offers two etymologies, one making the penitent understand afterwards, the other making the whole life of a sinner a continued course of madness, and recalls the Latin term for a growing wise again. Gill reads the call as aimed at particular errors, justification by works among the Pharisees and the expectation of a temporal kingdom among all. Lightfoot adds that the rabbis had themselves disputed whether Israel were to be redeemed with repentance or without it.

Ellicott notes that the kingdom of the heavens is peculiar to this evangelist, and thinks the other form preferred for readers who would hear only the visible firmament in it. Clarke supplies the imagery behind the herald from Diodorus, where Semiramis had the precipices of the Zarcean mountain dug down and its hollows filled to shorten her march. Calvin refuses to confine the prophecy to John, since the comfort promised after the temple fell was spoken to Zechariah and Haggai and Malachi before him.
4:
Almost everyone reads the dress as a deliberate citation of Elijah. Clarke notes that the coarse covering was common to the prophets and that Elijah wore it, and holds that John, designated under that prophet's name, took the same habit and the same self-denial. Ellicott makes the imitation conscious and sets it against two contemporary wardrobes, the long garments of the Pharisees and the gorgeous apparel of the scribes who attached themselves to the court of Herod, adding that the rough garment remained the prophet's mark long afterwards and that the Nazarite vow probably carried shaggy hair with it. Robertson quotes Plummer for the same judgment, that John consciously took Elijah as a model, though he thinks it necessity rather than affectation, and asks whether such an uncouth figure would be welcome in any city pulpit today.

Barnes is careful about the material, since the name misleads. This is not the fine hair from which the elegant cloth is made, nor the stuff brought from the East Indies under the same name, but the long shaggy hair woven into a coarse cheap cloth, still worn in the East by the poorer classes and by monks.

What he ate divides the commentators less than it might. Barnes treats the locusts as common people's food, notes that among the Greeks the vilest ate such things, and takes the detail as a mark of great poverty; he adds that the green kind runs about two inches and the brown about three, not unlike a grasshopper in form, and that they come in quantities enough to darken the sky. Ellicott confirms they were permitted by the law and are still eaten by the poor in Palestine and Syria, commonly salted and dried, pounded or fried in butter, and tasting like shrimps; and refuses to entertain the alternative, since it is needless, the facts being so clear, to find the Baptist's food in the sweet pods of the tree that bears the same name. Clarke gives that alternative its hearing before rejecting it, since the word may mean either the insect or the top of a plant and many eminent commentators have preferred the plant, but he judges the insect likelier and observes that the old Saxon translator put grasshoppers. He guesses the dried insects were fried in the honey, and reports that the Gospel according to the Hebrews, as Epiphanius quotes it, adds that the taste was like manna, a sweet cake baked in oil. Wesley notices that locusts rank among clean meats but were not always to be had, so the honey served in default of them; the girdle he takes for Elijah's, in whose spirit and power John came. Lightfoot supplies the rabbinic cross-check, that a man who binds himself by vow from flesh is thereby forbidden the flesh of fish and of locusts alike.

Calvin alone treats the whole description as a trap for the reader. The Evangelist does not want the rough living reckoned among John's chief excellencies, nor even his avoidance of a moderate elegance; having placed him in the mountains, he adds only that food and clothing suited the residence. The point, on Calvin's reading, is the reverse of the ascetic one: that under a mean and contemptible garb he was held in high estimation by men of rank and splendour. From there he turns on the reading he means to exclude. Superstitious persons make righteousness consist almost entirely of outward appearances and have commonly thought abstinence of this kind the perfection of holiness; near that error is the supposition that he lived in solitude and disdained the ordinary way of living, when the only superiority of hermits and monks is that they differ from other people. He ends by complaining that ignorance has gone so far as to make an entire skin out of what was only a girdle.
5:
Why such crowds came is answered three ways that do not compete. Gill lists the attractions in order, the uncommon appearance of the man, the oddness of his dress, the austerity of his life, the weight of his doctrine, the novelty of the rite, and behind all of it a nation without a prophet for some hundreds of years that half suspected this one of being the Messiah. Chrysostom sharpens two of these: they saw in him the great Elias, and the gift of prophecy long failed among them seemed at last revived; and the preaching was unlike anything they knew, since the old prophets had spoken of wars and the conquests of the kings of Babylon and Persia, while this man spoke of heaven and the kingdom there and the punishment of hell. Lightfoot answers from the calendar, that the manifestation was expected just then because Daniel's weeks were spent to the last four years, and he divides the four hundred and ninety years into seven weeks to the finishing of the city and sixty-two more to the opening of the last.

On the extent of the movement the commentators are careful with the word all. Barnes says it does not mean literally everyone but that the resort was general, and Gill says the same, that all is put for many. Ellicott takes the region round about to cover the whole river valley and so parts of four districts. Lightfoot finds the phrase in the Jerusalem Gemara, where the stretch from Beth-horon to the sea is called one circumjacent region, and compares Pliny's usage for a coast with the country lying along it.

What the rite was Barnes explains from its history. The word means first to tinge or dye, and so to cleanse by applying water; washings were already familiar among the Jews, who for some time before John had been administering one to Gentiles coming over to their religion, as a sign that they renounced the errors of the heathen and were made clean for a new service. John found the custom in use, and what was new was that he applied it to Jews. Ellicott notices the tense, a continual succession, crowd after crowd, and places the confession in the closest possible connection with the act itself; the word for confessing, he adds, always implies public utterance, and its plural suggests that particular sins, at least the graver ones, were named.

The manner of it is the one open quarrel, and it is fought on practical ground. Clarke puts the objections as questions. Can any man suppose it possible to dip all the inhabitants of Jerusalem and Judaea and the country round? Were women dipped as well as men, since both came? That could never have comported with safety or decency. Were they dipped in their clothes, at the risk of their lives, and is it likely such crowds came provided with dry raiment? Wesley presses the same objections and offers a reconstruction: they stood in ranks along the edge of the river and John, passing before them, cast water on their heads, by which he might baptize thousands in a day; and this, he argues, answers better to the pouring out of the Spirit that the rite prefigured. Robertson calls it a pity that baptism should now be a matter of controversy, and takes his ground from Plummer, that it was the Baptist's office to bind them to a new life symbolized by immersion, adding the qualification himself, symbolized and not caused.

Calvin is interested in the confession rather than the water. In the sacraments God binds himself to us as though he had given his hand-writing, and it is our part to reply; where that reply is absent the whole performance is an idle mockery. From this he draws his rule, that adults are not to be admitted indiscriminately but only after examination.
7:
The address changes when the audience does. Calvin makes it a rule of teaching, that instruction is unprofitable unless the instructor asks what the season demands and what belongs to the particular hearer, and that nothing is more unequal in this respect than a constant equality; the severity follows from hypocrites being the stupidest of men, deceiving themselves along with everyone else under an outward mask of holiness. Henry says the same more briefly, that application is the life of preaching: to others it was enough to say repent, but these needed closer dealing. Robertson observes where it happened, that John had welcomed the multitudes and then exposed the ecclesiastics in front of them, and he borrows the judgment that a strong attraction here and a strong repulsion there made the two parties forget their differences for the moment.

The sects themselves are described at length and not always alike. Clarke thinks the Pharisees were in their origin very probably a pure and holy people, named from separating themselves from the pollutions of the national worship; they degenerated afterwards, keeping the rules of their institution when the spirit was gone. The Sadducees he calls the materialists and deists of the Jewish nation. Barnes dates all the sects to about a hundred and fifty years before Christ, which is why the Old Testament knows nothing of them. Lightfoot contributes a philological correction: the name cannot come from the word meaning to expound, since there were women of the party as well as men, the rabbis having a saying about the woman-Pharisee among the things that destroy the world.

On the name John gives them Wesley argues that it is not abuse. Herod is called a fox, and men of insidious or sensual disposition serpents and dogs and wolves and swine; these are not the random language of passion but a judicious designation by one who saw their hearts. Augustine guards the other half of the sentence, that when Scripture speaks of wrath in God it describes him from a likeness of effects, the word belonging to the effects of his vengeance and not to any disturbance in him.

Two of the fathers answer the appeal to descent along the same line. Chrysostom points out that they are not forbidden to say they are Abraham's, only to trust in it while neglecting the virtues of the soul; that men should be made out of stones he finds no stranger than Isaac coming from Sarah's womb; the word every, he adds, cuts off all privilege of birth, so that the son of Abraham who stays fruitless suffers with the rest. Gregory puts the diagnosis first, that men who gloried in their race would not own themselves sinners, and then reads the axe as the Redeemer himself, of haft and blade as of two natures, held by the human and cutting by the divine.

What the fruits are divides on a point of grammar and one of substance. Ellicott complains that the English is ambiguous and not happy, since it suggests fruit that prepares the way for repentance when the sense is fruit worthy of a repentance already professed by coming. Robertson agrees, that the fruit is not the change of heart but the acts which follow from it, and that anyone can do externally good acts while only a good man grows a crop of them. Gregory presses the word meet hardest: a man who never fell into unlawful things may use all lawful ones, while one who has fallen ought to put away even lawful things so far as he used unlawful, the loss by sin measuring the gain to be sought by repentance. Wesley distinguishes the legal repentance meant here, a thorough conviction of sin, from the evangelical, a change of heart and life. Barnes keeps to the tone, that no discourse could have been more appropriate or more cutting.
9:
Ellicott says the boast was common, bound up with the belief that descent alone, or descent joined to the confession that the Lord our God is one Lord, would secure any Jew an entrance into Paradise; to the Jew, he adds, we have Abraham as our father was all that being a Roman citizen was to a Roman, and more. Wesley calls the presumption almost incredible and quotes a saying of theirs, that Abraham sits near the gates of hell and suffers no Israelite to go down into it. Gill describes the inward use of it, their pleasing themselves with the thought and repeating it as proof that they stood in favour and had a right to every privilege. Robertson says the words touched the tender spot, their ecclesiastical pride, and made the breach between preacher and leaders plain at once.

Lightfoot identifies the opening phrase as a Jerusalem idiom found everywhere in the Talmud, where to think a word means to be of that opinion. Calvin describes the psychology the rebuke assumes: until hypocrites are hard pressed they sleep in their sins or amuse themselves, and when summoned they cast about for some covering to interpose between themselves and God, the covenant serving as a shield for a bad conscience.

On the stones there is agreement about the gesture and a difference about the sense. Robertson and Wesley take the words as spoken with a hand pointing to the pebbles on the bank. Barnes draws the comparison out: God could more easily make worthy children of Abraham from these stones than make subjects of the kingdom out of the proud and hypocritical, so that birth avails nothing where life does not answer to it; Ellicott finds in the saying the germ of everything afterwards taught about the calling of the Gentiles.

The axe divides them more sharply, since it can figure several different things. Gill will not have it mean the gospel, though he grants that this cut down their self-confidence; he takes it for the judgment of God, laid not to some branches only but to the root of every privilege they had, and so to the covenant itself. Clarke and Lightfoot make it political: the prophets had long represented doomed nations as forests marked for felling, and here the nation is the tree and the Romans the axe; Lightfoot adds that the Talmud applies the same words to the destruction of the city, and argues from what follows there that the Messiah was to be born not long after. Barnes makes it a figure of the preaching itself, a searching kind of address now begun, in which men are tried by their lives and not their birth; they had made a fair profession, as trees do in blossom, and were now required to bear fruit as well as flowers. Calvin makes it the purging of the Church, and states a sequence he thinks general, that grace is never shown for the saving of the godly until judgment has first appeared for the destroying of the world.

On the urgency they agree, and two of them find the same picture in it. Clarke reads the words as leaving not a moment to spare, and describes a woodman who, having marked his tree, lays the axe at its root and strips off his outer garment so his blows may fall with full force; Wesley has the same figure. Robertson gets the urgency from the grammar, since the verb means the axe lies at the root already, there and ready for use, and the verbs following are prophetic presents. Ellicott puts it in one word, that now should rather be already, the present of an act no longer future; partial judgments had been the pruning of branches, and this leaves only preservation or destruction.
11:
Why a baptism that forgave nothing was administered at all is asked by three of the fathers. Gregory answers from the office: John could not remit sin, but the forerunner must go before in this as in his birth. Chrysostom answers from the sequence, that while the sacrifice was unoffered and the Spirit had not descended on the water there was no forgiveness to be had, so John's work was to bring a people who never perceived their sin to a sense of it. Augustine answers that John baptized because Christ was to be baptized by him; and asked why Christ was not then the only one, replies that some would have argued John's baptism the greater, since Christ alone had the merit to receive it.

The saying about the shoes is explained alike by everyone and documented differently. Barnes describes the sandal, a piece of wood or leather bound on by thongs, and says loosing and binding them was the work of the lowest servants, whose business it was to carry their master's about. Clarke calls it the work of the vilest slaves among Jews and Greeks and Romans alike, citing Arrian and the Babylonian Talmud. Lightfoot supplies the legal form: a servant could be bought by service, and the service sealing the purchase was this very one, loosening the buyer's shoe and carrying his things to the bath, so the sentence means whose servant I am not worthy to be. Ellicott adds that mightier looks two ways, to saving and to punishing, so the Coming One is at once Deliverer and Judge; Chrysostom denies any comparison is intended, since the speaker puts himself below the rank of a servant.

Calvin explains why the disclaimer was necessary: the people were in danger of transferring to John the honour due to Christ, and rather than let silence confirm them he declared outright that he was not the Christ.

On the promised baptism the emphasis falls on the preposition. Chrysostom notes that the words are not that he shall give the Holy Ghost but that he shall baptize in him, a metaphor for abundance; and from the ease of the outward rite he draws that under the faith the will alone justifies. Wesley reads the fire as love, not to be quenched by many waters, and points to its visible appearance at Pentecost. Robertson reports two constructions, Spirit and fire as a double baptism under one preposition, or fire in the sense of separation, like the fan that follows.

What the fan is divides them, and the division decides when the threshing happens. Gill offers the gospel and then prefers the judgment shortly to fall on the unbelieving nation, and describes the implement from the rabbis, three hand-shaped instruments with more or fewer teeth. Clarke is more particular: the Romans are God's fan here as they were his axe a moment ago, the floor is Judaea, and the wheat gathered into the garner he sees in the Christians sent to Pella before the city fell. Gregory puts the scene at the end instead, after the threshing of this life in which the grain groans under the chaff, when the fan of the last judgment will so divide them that no chaff passes into the granary and no grain falls into the fire. Robertson keeps to the coming of the Messiah, noticing that the verb means to sweep the floor clean from side to side. Ellicott grants the imagery was familiar from the prophets and marks what is new: the Coming One is himself the agent, the older picture stopped at the scattering while this goes on to the burning, and the fire is called unquenched. Calvin explains the order, grace first and judgment second, so that hypocrites who despised the author of salvation might dread him as an avenger.
13:
Henry marks the break. From childhood until now the Lord had lain hid in Galilee as if buried alive, and after a long dark night the Sun of righteousness rises; and he begins not at Jerusalem but where John was baptizing, because there had gathered the people who waited for the consolation of Israel. Gill reckons the interval at about six months.

Why a sinless man should come to a baptism of repentance is the question, and the answers do not agree. Ellicott will not pretend it is easy: the Sinless One had no sin to confess, yet his righteousness was human and therefore capable of increase, as he increased in wisdom and stature, so that height upon height of holiness rose before him, after which, he says with reverence, the Lord hungered and thirsted. Chrysostom argues from the Law. Christ was to end it after his baptism, and came at this age so that, having kept it, he could not be charged with cancelling what he had been unable to observe; against the scandal he says that the humiliation is where the exaltation shines, since the one amazement is that being God he would be made man, and the rest follows in course of reason. Augustine turns the act around: he was baptized not that he might be cleansed but that the water might be cleansed for us, and from the hour he was dipped in it he has washed our sins away in it; and lest anyone wonder that a corporeal substance should reach the soul, he answers that water is penetrating by nature and made more so by the blessing. Calvin keeps to the plainest ground, that Christ received the same baptism as we do to assure believers they are grafted into his body, and hears in the reply a deliberate setting aside of rank.

Whether John already knew him is a second question, and the witnesses divide. Gill holds that he did, not through kinship nor previous acquaintance but by immediate revelation, so that the descent of the Spirit confirmed a knowledge already given rather than supplying it. Robertson reads it the same way, the two meeting for the first time and the Baptist recognising the Coming One before the promised sign appears. Ellicott sets the difficulty out instead of solving it: this narrative seems to imply such knowledge, while the fourth Gospel asserts he did not know him until after the baptism; he supposes that look and tone and silence, rather than any communication, spoke of a stainless life. Calvin insists that John acknowledged him not as a distinguished prophet, as he says many foolishly dream, but as the Son of God; yet he finds John mistaken all the same, since the refusal was plausible only so long as he forgot that the baptism was asked for the sake of others.

The answer is read as a statement about timing and about office. Ellicott stresses the word now, since hereafter John would be the receiver and not the giver, while for the present each kept his place; and he notes that it becometh us covers both men, not the speaker only. Robertson says the explanation satisfied John, and that otherwise the Messiah would have seemed to hold aloof from his forerunner, so the two ministries are bound together by it. Clarke renders the phrase as every righteous ordinance and supports it from Justin Martyr, that Christ was circumcised and kept the other ordinances not for his own justification but to fulfil the dispensation committed to him. Wesley divides the duty, the one to receive the rite and the other to administer it. Barnes observes that no precept of the older law required this, so what was given was the sanction of an example, and adds a second purpose, that the occasion served for God to declare publicly whom he had appointed.
16:
Who saw and heard any of this is the first disagreement. Ellicott holds that the Lord and the Baptist alone perceived it, and says there is not the slightest ground for supposing a manifestation to anyone else. Clarke reads the grammar the same way, that the heavens were opened to John and John saw the Spirit lighting on Jesus. Barnes takes the opposite view of the voice, that it was probably heard by everyone present and was a public declaration. Calvin divides the benefit: since the Evangelists say John saw the Spirit, the sight was chiefly for his sake, though Christ also, so far as he was man, gained from it a further certainty of his calling.

On the opening of the heavens Calvin allows a real parting of the visible sky, so that John could see beyond the planets, but refuses to inquire further, since it is enough that it was a symbol of the divine presence.

The form of the descent divides them again, and the division is sharp. Clarke reports that some refer the likeness of a dove to a hovering motion rather than the shape of the bird, and rejects that as far-fetched and unsupported by the terms of the text. Wesley holds precisely the reading Clarke rejects, a glorious appearance of fire, perhaps in the shape of a dove, descending with a hovering motion until it rested on him. Chrysostom asks not about the appearance but why there was one: in the beginnings of spiritual things visible signs are given for those who can form no idea of what has no body. He adds the older history the bird recalls, that in the flood a dove brought the olive branch and tidings of rest, so now a dove points out the liberator and brings, for a branch, the adoption of the human race.

Augustine is careful about what such a sending means: the Spirit is said to be sent when an appearance is created for the time in which he may be visibly shown, and it is this visible operation, not any change in his invisible substance, that the word describes.

On the voice Augustine marks what is new: the Father taught by Moses and the prophets in type that the Son should come, and now shows him already come. He then offers an analogy: in their own substance the Three are One without interval of place or time, but in a speaker's mouth they are three separate words that cannot be uttered at once, and in writing each fills its own place; by that comparison one may understand how a Trinity indivisible in itself can be shown dividedly in a visible creation. Clarke and Wesley both take the episode as proof of the doctrine, Wesley naming the parts: the Father speaking, the Son spoken to, the Spirit descending.

Lightfoot and Gill turn to what the rabbis made of heavenly voices, and neither is impressed. Lightfoot observes that no voice is found sent from heaven between the giving of the law and this baptism, and takes what the Jews relate of the daughter of the voice partly for fables and partly for something worse; their own tradition has the Holy Spirit departing from Israel after the last prophets and this used instead, and he asks why prophecy should have been withdrawn if heavenly oracles were to continue. Gill reads the same stories as a device to make such voices seem common. On the closing words Ellicott notes that the tense points to a definite act rather than a continuing acceptance, and that the term for a beloved son is the one the Greek Old Testament uses where the English has only. Barnes takes it as a constant delight, Robertson as a timeless aorist, and Wesley asks what praise could stand beside it.
